title: Black Hoof, the Shawnee warrior who chose peace
summary: Black Hoof (Catecahassa), a Mekoche Shawnee born about 1740, fought Kentucky's settlers for decades, then led the Ohio Shawnee toward peace, farming and diplomacy. He kept most of his people out of Tecumseh's War and never signed a removal treaty.
bodyMarkdown:
Few men fought Kentucky's settlers longer than Catecahassa, the Shawnee the Americans called [Black Hoof](/people/#black-hoof). Fewer still made the turn he made in old age, from war chief to the Shawnee nation's leading voice for peace.

## Born a Mekoche

He was [born around 1740 into the Mekoche division of the Shawnee](https://grokipedia.com/page/black_hoof), one of the nation's [five divisions](/stories/shawnee-chillicothe-divisions/). As a child he may have traveled with [Peter Chartier's](/people/#peter-chartier) band of about 400 Shawnee, who between 1745 and 1748 founded Eskippakithiki, in what is now Clark County. It was the last Native town in Kentucky. The band moved on to Alabama and finally to the Illinois country.

## Forty years of war

Black Hoof grew into one of the most feared warriors of his nation. He is said to have [fought with the French](https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=16971) against [Braddock](/people/#edward-braddock) in 1755, and he is credited with fighting at Point Pleasant in 1774 and with riding in Capt. Henry Bird's 1780 invasion, when [Ruddell's Station](/stories/isaac-ruddell-and-the-guns-at-ruddells-station/) and Martin's Station surrendered to British cannon. He likely fought at the [1778 siege of Boonesborough](/stories/col-richard-callaway-of-boonesborough/) and in the 1779 defense of Chillicothe against [John Bowman](/stories/col-john-bowman-at-old-chillicothe/), though the details of his part are unclear.

He was in the fights against Josiah Harmar in 1790 and Arthur St. Clair in 1791. A U.S. Army officer later said that few living warriors had been in as many battles.

That ended at Fallen Timbers in 1794, when [Anthony Wayne](/people/#anthony-wayne)'s army broke the Native confederacy. The next summer Black Hoof [signed the Treaty of Greenville](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shawnee), which gave up much of what is now Ohio and [ended the long war for Kentucky](/stories/treaty-of-greenville-1795-the-line-to-the-kentucky-river/).

## The turn to peace

Black Hoof decided that fighting on would destroy his people. Like [Little Turtle](/stories/little-turtle-and-hardins-defeat-1790/) of the Miami, he concluded that the Shawnee had to adapt to survive. As head civil chief he became their spokesman with the United States. He delivered an [address](https://grokipedia.com/page/black_hoof) to President [Jefferson](/people/#thomas-jefferson) in February 1802 and made another journey to Washington in 1807–08.

He invited Quakers to teach farming, and in 1809 they [opened a mission at Wapakoneta](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wapakoneta,_Ohio), with a mill and a school.

When [Tecumseh](/stories/tecumseh-falls-at-the-thames-oct-5-1813/) and his brother, the Prophet, called the tribes to a new confederacy, Black Hoof [refused the Prophet's authority](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shawnee). He kept most of the Shawnee out of Tecumseh's War, which became part of the War of 1812, and sided with the Americans. In 1813 a man shot him in the face during a visit to Fort McArthur; he [survived and recovered fully](https://archive.shelbycountyhistory.org/schs/indians/chiefblackhoof.htm). In 1817 he signed the Treaty of Fort Meigs, which left the Shawnee three small reservations in Ohio.

## Kentucky today

He never signed a removal treaty. He led his people until he [died at his town, now Saint Johns, Ohio, in 1831](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Hoof), and the next year the Ohio Shawnee were moved west. His portrait, first published in [McKenney](/people/#thomas-l-mckenney) and [Hall's](/people/#james-hall-author) *History of the Indian Tribes of North America* in 1837, is shown here as printed in the 1842 edition. The map does not pin him, because no Kentucky site can be tied to him with confidence.
